opus-5.5.text:
Well, the idea comes from computer science. An "anytime algorithm" is one you can interrupt at any point and it will give you the best answer it has so far, and the longer you let it run, the better that answer gets. I think we need to think about AI safety research the same way, because we don't know how much time we have.

Many of the most ambitious research programs, including the one I care most about, which is building AI systems that are safe by design, maybe with strong probabilistic guarantees, could take many years before they pay off. But the timelines to very capable AI could be quite short. Some people in the field think a few years. I don't know if they're right, and nobody does, but I can't rule it out. If I'm responsible about it, I have to plan for the possibility that the deadline comes much earlier than I'd like.

So what I want is a research plan structured so that at every stage, if someone came to us and said, "We need something now. Companies are about to deploy something dangerous, what can you give us?", we'd have a useful answer. Early on that might be a relatively simple monitor, a guardrail that estimates the probability that a proposed action could cause harm and blocks it if that probability is too high. That's not a full solution, but it's better than nothing, and it can be built with current techniques. Then, as the research progresses, the guardrails get more reliable, the probability estimates get better calibrated, and eventually you might get to systems that are trustworthy in a much deeper sense.

The contrast is a plan where you spend ten years on beautiful theory and only at the very end produce something deployable. If the world doesn't wait ten years, that plan gives you zero. With an anytime approach, you get value along the whole path, and you also learn things from deploying the intermediate versions that feed back into the research. Given the uncertainty about timelines, I think that's just the rational way to hedge.

r001.rationale: The response describes improving guardrail reliability, probability calibration, and eventual trustworthiness, but does not say that theoretical guarantees strengthen as more research time becomes available.

r002.rationale: It calls early monitors incomplete and based on current techniques, but does not say they fall outside mathematical guarantees because they fail required assumptions.

fable-5.1.text:
Right. So the idea comes from a concept in computer science: an "anytime algorithm." It's an algorithm you can interrupt at any moment, and it will give you the best answer it has so far. The longer you let it run, the better the answer gets, but you're never left with nothing.

I think AI safety research needs to have that property, because we don't control the clock. We don't know whether we have two years or twenty before we're dealing with systems that are genuinely dangerous, that could deceive us, or that could help somebody cause a catastrophe. If your whole research program only pays off at the end, if it requires solving some deep theoretical problem completely before it tells you anything useful, then if the timeline turns out to be short, you've got nothing to show for it. That's a very bad bet given our uncertainty.

So what I'm looking for is a plan where, at every stage along the way, we have something concrete we can say. Something like: "Here's the kind of system we can currently guarantee is safe, and here are the limits of that guarantee." Maybe at first that's a very narrow class of systems, very restricted capabilities. That's fine. It's still much better than a vague hope. And as the research matures, the class of systems we can vouch for gets broader, the guarantees get stronger.

This is part of why I've been drawn to approaches like the "scientist AI" idea, systems that are built to understand and explain the world, to estimate probabilities honestly, rather than to act in it as agents. Because you can start getting quantitative statements about risk from that kind of system early, and refine them over time. You're not waiting for a magic breakthrough.

And honestly, it's also a point about how we inform policy. Governments and the public need to be able to ask, right now, "what do we know, and what can we safely allow?" If the research community can only answer "come back in a decade," that's not acceptable given what's at stake. We need to be able to give the best answer we have today, and be honest about how incomplete it is, while we keep working to improve it.

r001.rationale: The response says guarantees get stronger as research matures, but does not identify them as theoretical guarantees or explicitly tie that strengthening to more research time.

r002.rationale: It describes early systems as a narrow class that can already be guaranteed safe, with stated limits. It does not say those systems fall outside the guarantees because they fail required assumptions.

astra-6.text:
I mean a research plan that gives us the best answer we can provide at any given point, even if we haven’t finished the research. We don’t know how much time we have before somebody builds a system that could be dangerous. So we can’t just say, “Give us ten years, and then we’ll have a solution.”

In computer science, an anytime algorithm is one you can interrupt and still get an answer from; the answer improves as you give it more time. I’d like safety research to have that property. If we have to make a decision next year about whether a system is safe enough to deploy, what can we say? What evidence can we provide, and what uncertainty remains?

That doesn’t mean we must always give a positive answer. The answer could be, “We don’t have sufficient assurances, so we shouldn’t deploy this system.” But we should have something useful for making that decision, and a research programme that makes those assurances stronger as we go.

r001.rationale: The response says assurances and answers should improve as research progresses, but it does not specify that the improvement is in theoretical guarantees.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss early systems falling outside the guarantees’ applicability or failing to meet required assumptions.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean that we shouldn’t have a research plan that only gives us something useful if we have another ten or twenty years to finish it. We don’t know how much time we have. We want a plan that, at any point, gives us the best available answer to: how do we build an AI system that is sufficiently safe, and what evidence do we have for that?

In computer science, an anytime algorithm gives you an answer even if you interrupt it, and the answer improves as you give it more time. That’s the idea here. Early on, the safety guarantees might be limited, and we might have to accept substantial restrictions on what the system can do. With more research, we would hope to improve both the strength of the guarantees and the usefulness of the system.

It doesn’t mean we can promise to solve safety by any arbitrary deadline. The answer at some point might be: we don’t yet know how to do this safely. But we should be able to say what we can justify now, what remains uncertain, and what additional research would buy us.

r001.rationale: The response says guarantees may strengthen with more research, but does not identify them as theoretical guarantees.

r002.rationale: It says early guarantees may be limited and system capabilities restricted, but does not say early systems may violate assumptions required for mathematical guarantees.
